Before you can protect your supply, you must see it. In this module you list every material in your product, trace where each one really comes from, rank materials by value and risk, and write the specifications and buying rules that every supplier and helper must follow.

A **supply chain** is every step a material passes through before it becomes part of your product: the farm or factory that makes it, the wholesaler or importer who moves it in bulk, the market trader who sells it to you, the transport that brings it to your door, and your own store. When you buy from whoever has stock that day, you only see the last step. Supply chain management starts when you deliberately look at all of them.

At small scale, a missing material is an inconvenience. Once customers, shops or institutions depend on your output, a missing material becomes a broken promise. A supermarket that receives no delivery for two weeks may give your shelf space to someone else. This course is about making that kind of failure rare, planned for and quickly fixed.

Step one: the bill of materials

A **bill of materials** (often shortened to BOM) is a list of every input needed to make one unit or one batch of your product, with the quantity and cost of each. Manufacturers everywhere use it. It answers two questions at once: what exactly do I need to buy, and which materials take the biggest share of my cost?
Worked example: a bill of materials for zobo drinks

Amaka, for example, makes bottled zobo in Enugu and sells about 600 bottles of 50cl a week to offices and small shops. She works in batches of 100 bottles. Prices below are illustrative and approximate; use your own current market prices.
Dried hibiscus (zobo leaves): 1.5 kg at about ₦3,000 per kg = ₦4,500
Sugar: 4 kg at about ₦1,800 per kg = ₦7,200
Fresh ginger: 0.5 kg at about ₦2,000 per kg = ₦1,000
50cl PET bottles with caps: 100 at about ₦60 each = ₦6,000
Printed labels: 100 at about ₦25 each = ₦2,500
Total materials per batch = ₦21,200, so materials cost ₦212 per bottle

Amaka now sees that sugar and bottles together are about 62% of her material cost. A price rise or shortage in either one hits her harder than a problem with ginger.

Notice what the BOM leaves out on purpose: gas, water, labour and transport. Those are real costs, and you will add transport into the true cost of materials in Module 2. For mapping, keep the BOM to physical inputs that go into or onto the product.
Step two: trace each material through its tiers

Supply chain people talk about **tiers**. Your **tier 1** supplier is the person you pay directly, for example a trader at the main market. **Tier 2** is who supplies that trader, for example a wholesaler or a factory distributor. **Tier 3** may be the farm, the processor or the foreign manufacturer. You rarely control tiers 2 and 3, but you must know they exist, because a problem there reaches you a few days or weeks later.

Decide where to spend your limited time on suppliers

You cannot give every material the same attention. A busy owner has limited hours, limited cash and limited patience for market trips. Two simple tools, used by purchasing professionals worldwide, tell you where your attention pays off: **ABC analysis**, which ranks materials by how much money you spend on them, and the **Kraljic matrix**, which adds a second question: how risky is the supply?
ABC analysis: follow the money

List every material with its total spend over a year (or estimate: monthly spend multiplied by 12). Sort from highest to lowest and calculate each one's share of the total. A common rule of thumb is that a few items make up most of the spend. Class **A** items are the top ones that together make up roughly 70 to 80% of spend. Class **B** items make up the next 15 to 25%. Class **C** items are the many small items that make up the last few percent. The exact cut-offs are a guide, not a law.
Worked example: ABC analysis for a uniform workshop
Bisi, for example, runs a tailoring workshop in Ibadan that sews uniforms for three private schools. Her estimated yearly material spend is ₦3,200,000 (figures illustrative).
School-colour check fabric: ₦1,500,000, which is 46.9% of spend
White shirting fabric: ₦900,000, which is 28.1%. Running total: 75.0%
Interlining: ₦210,000 (6.6%), buttons: ₦180,000 (5.6%), thread: ₦150,000 (4.7%). Running total: about 91.9%
Zips: ₦120,000 (3.8%), poly bags for packing: ₦90,000 (2.8%), elastic: ₦50,000 (1.6%). Running total: 100%
Class A: the two fabrics. Class B: interlining, buttons, thread. Class C: zips, bags, elastic
Two materials out of eight carry 75% of Bisi's spend. A 5% better price on fabric saves about ₦120,000 a year, while a 5% better price on elastic saves only ₦2,500.

ABC alone can mislead you. Bisi's zips are a C item by spend, but if the school insists on one zip colour that only one importer stocks, running out of zips stops delivery just as surely as running out of fabric. That is why you add the second question.
The Kraljic matrix: value and risk together

In 1983 Peter Kraljic published an article in the Harvard Business Review arguing that purchasing should become supply management. His matrix places each material on two scales. **Profit impact**: how much it affects your cost and product quality (your ABC class is a good starting point). **Supply risk**: how hard it is to get, judged by the number of suppliers, how easy it is to substitute, transport problems, imports and price swings.

Single sourcing or dual sourcing?

**Single sourcing** means buying a material from one supplier. It can earn you better attention and price, but it leaves you exposed. **Dual sourcing** means keeping two active suppliers, perhaps buying most from one and a smaller share from the other so the second relationship stays alive. For leverage items, dual sourcing is easy and keeps prices honest. For strategic items, you often have to choose a main partner and invest in the relationship, yet you should still test and approve a backup before a crisis, not during one.
Your scores are judgements

There is no official score for supply risk. Use what you know: how many sellers you have found, whether it is imported, whether it is seasonal, and how often it has been out of stock. Review the matrix every six months, because a material can move. A new local factory can turn a bottleneck into a non-critical item.

Many quality problems start with a vague order. 'Bring me good shea butter' means something different to every trader. A **material specification** (spec) is a short written description of exactly what you accept. It protects you when you change suppliers, when a helper buys on your behalf, and when you need to reject a bad delivery without an argument.
What goes into a specification
**Name and type**: the exact material, grade or variety, and any brand you require
**Appearance, smell and feel**: what a good sample looks like, and what is unacceptable
**Measurable limits**: size, weight, width, thickness or other numbers you can check with simple tools
**Packaging**: container type, size, sealing and labelling, including supplier batch or lot number where one exists
**Documents**: invoice or receipt, and for regulated materials any certificate the product requires
**Delivery**: where, when, and how much notice you need
**Reference sample**: a retained sample you both agree represents the standard
A clipboard with a written list
A one-page spec turns 'good quality' into something anyone can check.
Worked example: a spec for shea butter

Funke, for example, makes whipped body butter in Lagos and uses about 20 kg of shea butter a month. Twice she received butter with grit and a sour smell. She writes this spec and sends it on WhatsApp to every supplier before ordering.
Material: unrefined shea butter, for cosmetic use
Appearance: ivory to pale yellow, smooth, no visible dirt, sand, fibres or water drops
Smell: mild and nutty. Reject if sour, rancid or smoky
Packaging: clean, sealed, food-grade plastic buckets of 5 kg or 25 kg, with the packing date written on the lid
Reference: one 250 g jar from an approved delivery kept in her store as the standard
Trial for a new supplier: buy 5 kg, melt and strain 1 kg, weigh what is left in the strainer, and make one small batch of product before approving
Result of a trial: 1,000 g melted, 100 g of grit and residue in the strainer, so 10% waste. Her approved supplier's residue was about 10 g, or 1%
Funke can now compare suppliers on facts. The new supplier's butter wastes ten times as much, which she will price into her comparison in Module 2.

Notice that Funke did not invent laboratory numbers she cannot test. A small producer's spec should use checks she can actually do: look, smell, weigh, measure with a tape, count, or run a small test batch. If your product is regulated, NAFDAC or SON requirements for the finished product come first, and your spec must make sure every input lets you meet them. For example, a cosmetic or food producer should only use materials meant for that use, not industrial grades.
Chemical materials need extra rules

If you buy chemicals such as caustic soda, acids, solvents or fragrance oils, add to your spec: original sealed container, clear product name and hazard label, and a safety data sheet (SDS) where the supplier can provide one. Never accept a chemical repacked into an unlabelled water bottle or food container. Store chemicals away from food materials and out of reach of children.

Most stockouts are not caused by the supplier alone. They happen because the order was placed too late. The **reorder point** is the stock level that tells you: order now. If you order when stock falls to that level, the new delivery should arrive before you run out, even on a bad week.
Three numbers you need
**Usage rate**: how much you use per working day. Use your production records, not a guess.

**Lead time**: the number of working days from the moment you place the order to the moment the material is in your store and checked. Include the time you wait for the supplier to restock, transport, and your own inspection.
**Safety stock**: extra stock you hold to cover days when usage is higher or delivery is slower than normal.

Look back at your last six to ten orders for the material. For each one, count the days from order to usable stock. The average of those is your **average lead time**. The longest one is your **maximum lead time**. Do the same for daily usage: your normal day and your busiest day. A supplier's promise of 'two days' is not your lead time; your records are.
An hourglass with sand flowing
Lead time is the sand running out: your stock must last until the new delivery is ready to use.
The formulas

A simple, widely taught way to set safety stock when you do not have much data is the **max-minus-average** method: safety stock = (maximum daily usage x maximum lead time) minus (average daily usage x average lead time). Then the **reorder point** = (average daily usage x average lead time) + safety stock. More advanced methods use statistics, but this version works well for a small business with a notebook and a few months of records.
Worked example: reorder point for bottles

Amaka, for example, fills an average of 100 bottles a day over six working days. On her busiest days she fills 140. From her last eight bottle orders, delivery took 5 working days on average and 8 days at worst.
Normal demand during lead time: 100 bottles x 5 days = 500 bottles
Worst-case demand during lead time: 140 bottles x 8 days = 1,120 bottles
Safety stock: 1,120 minus 500 = 620 bottles
Reorder point: 500 + 620 = 1,120 bottles
Cash tied up in safety stock at about ₦60 per bottle: 620 x ₦60 = ₦37,200
When Amaka's bottle count falls to 1,120, she orders. On a normal week about 620 bottles will still be on the shelf when the delivery arrives; in the worst week she just avoids running out.

Notice that with this method the reorder point equals maximum usage multiplied by maximum lead time. It is cautious on purpose. If the ₦37,200 tied up in safety stock is too much for your cash, you can choose a smaller buffer, but then write down the risk you are accepting.

Recalculate every few months, and whenever something changes: a new supplier, a big new customer, or a route that has become slower. A reorder point built on last year's usage will be too low once your sales grow, and that is exactly when a stockout hurts most.

How much to order each time

The reorder point tells you **when** to order. How much depends on the supplier's minimum order, pack sizes, your storage space, shelf life and cash. A practical rule is to order enough for a fixed period, for example two or four weeks of normal usage, rounded to full packs. Amaka uses 600 bottles a week, so two weeks is 1,200 bottles. Larger orders may earn a discount, which you will weigh in Lesson 3 of this module.
Put it in a sheet

In Google Sheets or Excel, make one row per material with columns: A material, B average daily use, C average lead time, D maximum daily use, E maximum lead time, F safety stock, G reorder point, H current stock, I status. In F2 type =D2*E2-B2*C2. In G2 type =B2*C2+F2. In I2 type =IF(H2<=G2,"ORDER NOW","OK"). Update column H each Friday after counting, and the sheet tells you what to buy.
The two-bin system for small items

For cheap non-critical items such as thread, labels or cable ties, counting is wasted effort. Use **two bins**: keep stock in two containers, and use only from the first. When the first bin is empty, that is your reorder signal; you work from the second bin while the new stock comes. Make each bin hold at least enough for one lead time plus a little extra.
Seasonal and imported materials

For crops harvested once a year, or materials that come by sea, lead time and price change through the year. Ask your supplier which months are hardest, and plan larger orders before those months rather than using one fixed reorder point all year.

A material problem found at the gate costs you a phone call. The same problem found after production costs you the whole batch, and if it reaches a customer, your reputation. The **receiving check** is the moment you compare what arrived with what you ordered and with your spec from Module 1.
A person receiving a package at the door
Every delivery is checked before it joins your stock.
A six-step receiving check
**Match the paperwork**: compare the delivery note or receipt with your order: material, quantity, price.
**Count or weigh**: count cartons and weigh a few bags on your own scale. A 25 kg bag that weighs 23.5 kg is short by 6%.
**Inspect packaging**: seals intact, no water damage, no torn bags, labels readable, batch or packing date present.
**Check a sample against the spec**: open several containers from different parts of the load, not just the top one, and compare with your reference sample.
**Decide**: accept, accept with a note, or reject. Put doubtful stock in a marked 'HOLD' area, separate from usable stock, until the supplier responds.
**Record**: write the date, supplier, quantity, batch, result and who checked.

Complain with evidence, quickly

Take photos of short weight on the scale, damaged packs or contamination before you move anything, and send them to the supplier the same day. A complaint a week later, with no photos, is easy to dispute.

Agree the rules for rejected material before the first order, not during the argument. Who collects the rejected goods, and who pays the transport? Will the supplier replace the material, or credit the value against your next order? How many days do you have to report a problem found only when you open the inner bags? Write the answers in your supplier notes or confirm them in a WhatsApp message, so both sides can refer back to them.
Storing materials properly
**FIFO and FEFO**: first in, first out, or for materials with expiry dates, first expired, first out. Put new stock behind old stock.
**Off the floor**: keep sacks and cartons on pallets or shelves, away from walls, to reduce damp and pests.
**Cool, dry, shaded**: heat and humidity spoil oils, sugar, flour and many packaging materials.
**Separate**: keep chemicals, cleaning products and fuel well apart from food or cosmetic materials.
**Label**: each container shows the material, supplier, date received and batch.
Traceability: linking batches

**Traceability** means you can say which supplier delivery went into which of your product batches. Give each production batch a code, for example the date plus a letter, and in your production record write the supplier batch or delivery date of each key material used. If a customer complains, you can find the material, check the remaining stock, and talk to the supplier with facts. Larger buyers and regulators increasingly expect this, and it costs only a column in your notebook.
Scoring suppliers on facts

Memory is unfair to suppliers: we remember the last bad delivery and forget ten good ones. The standard measure is **on time in full (OTIF)**: the percentage of deliveries that arrived by the agreed date with the full quantity and passed inspection. If 9 of 12 deliveries met all three conditions, OTIF is 9 divided by 12, which is 75%.

The cheapest price per kilogram is often not the cheapest material. **Total cost of ownership** (TCO) adds everything it costs you to get a material into production: the price, transport, minimum order effects, waste, extra labour, and the cost of late or failed deliveries. Purchasing professionals compare suppliers on TCO, and so should you.
Landed cost per usable unit

Start with **landed cost**: price plus every cost of getting the material to your door, such as transport, loading, market levies and transfer charges. Then divide by the quantity you can actually use after waste. That gives the **cost per usable unit**, the figure that matters for your product costing.
Worked example: two shea butter suppliers
Funke, for example, compares her Lagos trader with a cheaper processor in the north. She orders 25 kg at a time. Prices are illustrative.
Supplier A (Lagos): ₦2,500 per kg, free delivery. 25 x ₦2,500 = ₦62,500. Waste after straining 1%, so 24.75 kg usable
A's cost per usable kg: ₦62,500 divided by 24.75 = about ₦2,525
Supplier B (north): ₦2,000 per kg, plus ₦7,500 transport. 25 x ₦2,000 + ₦7,500 = ₦57,500
B's waste after straining is 10% (her trial showed grit), so 22.5 kg usable. Extra straining time she values at ₦2,000. Total ₦59,500
B's cost per usable kg: ₦59,500 divided by 22.5 = about ₦2,644
B was also late on 2 of her last 6 orders, which forced emergency buying at a higher price

The supplier that looked 20% cheaper is about ₦119 more expensive per usable kilogram, before counting late deliveries. Funke stays with A, and tells B she would reconsider if the butter came cleaner.

Is a quantity discount worth it?

Suppose Supplier A offers ₦2,350 per kg if Funke buys 50 kg instead of 25 kg. Saving: ₦150 x 50 = ₦7,500. But she must pay ₦117,500 at once instead of ₦62,500, so ₦55,000 more cash leaves her business early and sits on the shelf for an extra month. Ask three questions: Do I have the cash without starving other needs? Will the material keep well for that long in my storage conditions? Do I have space? If all three answers are yes, the discount is worth taking. If cash is tight, ₦7,500 is not worth missing a profitable order elsewhere.

Negotiating with suppliers
Price is only one lever. Small producers often gain more from the other ones, and suppliers find them easier to give. Before you talk, decide what you want on each:
**Price tiers**: what price at 25 kg, 50 kg, 100 kg?
**Payment terms**: for example half on order and half on delivery, or a few days' credit once trust is built
**Delivery**: fixed delivery day, delivery included, or a faster option for emergencies
**Quality guarantee**: replacement or credit for material that fails the agreed spec
**Priority**: a promise to reserve stock for you during shortages, in return for regular orders

Your strongest preparation is your **BATNA**, the best alternative to a negotiated agreement. It comes from the Harvard negotiation tradition. In sourcing, your BATNA is usually your approved backup supplier and their price. If you know you can buy at ₦2,550 elsewhere, you can calmly decline a rise to ₦2,700. Without a backup, you have no real alternative, and the supplier can sense it. This is one more reason the backup work in Module 1 pays off.
Running the conversation
**Prepare**: write your expected volume for the next three months, your BATNA, the price you hope for and the point at which you will walk away.
**Open with facts and the relationship**: 'I have bought from you every month this year and I expect to double my volume from January.'
**Ask open questions**: 'What would it take to get a better price at 50 kg?' Let the supplier propose first.
**Trade, do not just take**: if they move on price, offer something they value, such as a fixed order day, faster payment or a longer commitment.
**Confirm in writing**: send a short WhatsApp summary of what was agreed the same day, and keep it with your supplier notes.
Protect your money and records

Pay by bank transfer or through a traceable channel such as a business account on Moniepoint, OPay or your bank app, and keep every receipt. Confirm the account name matches the supplier before sending. If a supplier suddenly asks you to pay into a different account, call them on the number you already know before paying.

Growing a Resilient Supply Chain

With the basics in place, you can grow. This module covers buying closer to the source, pooling orders with other producers, the basics of importing, handing purchasing to a trusted person with proper controls, and building the risk register and 90-day plan that make your supply chain resilient.

Each layer between you and the source adds a margin and a delay. Buying closer to the source, for example from a processor, a factory distributor or directly from abroad, can lower your price and give you better information about quality and availability. It also brings new demands: bigger minimum orders, more cash paid earlier, longer lead times and more of the risk on your side.

Neither is always better; move closer to the source only when your volume and cash can carry it.

Buying direct makes sense when three things are true: your volume is steady enough to meet the minimum order, you have the cash and storage for larger lots, and the saving remains after you add transport, waste and your own time. If one of the three is missing, a reliable trader is often the better partner.
Group purchasing

If your volume is too small to buy direct, combine it with other producers. A **group purchase** (or buying cooperative) lets several small businesses order together to reach a bulk price, while each stays independent. It works when members use the same material to the same spec and trust the arrangements, which must be written down.

Some materials, such as certain packaging, machinery parts, fragrance oils or speciality ingredients, may be cheaper or only available abroad. International trade uses the **Incoterms rules** published by the International Chamber of Commerce (the current set is Incoterms 2020) to state who pays for what and where risk passes from seller to buyer. Importing also exposes you to **exchange-rate risk**. For illustration, if a supplier quotes $2,000 and the rate is ₦1,500 to the dollar, the goods cost ₦3,000,000. If the naira weakens by 10% to ₦1,650 before you pay, the same goods cost ₦3,300,000, an extra ₦300,000 before any freight or duty. Build a margin for this into your costing, and check the current rate on the day you pay.
Check rules before you import

Some imported products must meet Standards Organisation of Nigeria (SON) conformity requirements, and food, cosmetic and chemical inputs may fall under NAFDAC rules. Ask your bank about the documentation needed for foreign payments, and speak with a licensed customs agent before your first order. Never pay a foreign supplier you have not verified, and start with a sample shipment.

The answer is not to avoid delegating. It is to delegate with a clear process and simple controls, the way established companies do.

**Separation of duties** is a basic internal control: the person who places an order should not be the only person who confirms it arrived, and ideally not the one who pays. In a two-person business, it can be as simple as: your buyer orders, you or another person counts the delivery against the order, and payment goes out from the business account only after the count matches.

**Resilience** is your supply chain's ability to keep production going when something goes wrong, and to recover quickly when it cannot. You cannot prevent fuel price jumps, road closures or a factory breakdown. You can know in advance which of these would hurt most and prepare a response. The tool for this is a **risk register**.

Scoring risks

List what could go wrong with each critical material: supplier stops trading, price jumps, quality drops, transport is disrupted, the material becomes seasonal or scarce. Give each risk two scores from 1 (low) to 5 (high): **likelihood**, how probable it is in the next year, and **impact**, how badly it would hurt production, quality or profit. Multiply them. A score of 15 or more needs action now; 8 to 14 needs a plan; below 8 you watch.

One clearly chosen risk, worked on week by week, beats a long list nobody acts on.

This is the video for module one of Supply Chain and Raw Materials Sourcing.
Why this matters
A missing material is a broken promise
Know every material in your product
Trace where each one really comes from
Rank materials by value and risk
Write down exactly what you accept
A supply chain is every step a material passes through before it becomes your product: farm or factory, wholesaler, trader, transport, and your store.
Once customers depend on you, a missing material becomes a broken promise.
So first, you trace where each material really comes from.
Then you rank materials by value and risk, and write down exactly what you will accept.
Step one
A bill of materials for zobo
For example, Amaka makes bottled zobo in Enugu, in batches of 100 bottles of 50cl.
Hibiscus, 1.5 kg
Sugar, 4 kg
Ginger, 0.5 kg
100 bottles with caps
100 printed labels
Naira prices are illustrative and approximate.
A bill of materials, or BOM, lists every input for one batch, with quantity and cost.
Amaka makes zobo in batches of 100 bottles. Her prices are illustrative and approximate.
Dried hibiscus costs about 4,500 naira, sugar 7,200, and fresh ginger 1,000.
100 bottles with caps cost about 6,000 naira, and 100 labels 2,500.
That is 21,200 naira per batch, or 212 naira per bottle.
Sugar and bottles together are about 62% of her material cost, so a problem with either one hits her harder than a problem with ginger.
Step two
Trace each material through its tiers
The person you pay directly, for example a trader at the main market.
Who supplies your trader, for example a wholesaler or factory distributor.
The farm, the processor or the foreign manufacturer.
Your tier 1 supplier is the person you pay directly.
Tier 2 is who supplies that trader, such as a wholesaler.
Tier 3 may be the farm or the factory. You rarely control them, but a problem there reaches you days or weeks later.
So ask your trader where it comes from. Amaka learned her bottles come from one distributor of a single factory.
Step three
Is this material critical?
Can I make the product without it?
Can I switch source within one week?
Would customers notice a change?
Circle any branch with only one supplier
A material is critical if you cannot produce without it and cannot quickly swap it. Ask three questions. Can I make the product without it?
Can I switch to another source within one week? Amaka cannot: her labels and caps fit only her bottle.
Would customers notice a change? If yes, a substitute carries quality risk.
One supplier whose absence would stop production is a single point of failure. If only your printer holds your label design, the fix is free: keep your own copy and share it with a second printer.
Rank by value and risk
Four boxes for your materials
Strategic: partner, backup, safety stock
Leverage: compare quotes, negotiate
Bottleneck: extra stock or second source
Non-critical: keep buying simple
First rank materials by yearly spend. This is ABC analysis. In Bisi's uniform workshop, two fabrics out of eight materials carry 75% of her spend.
Then add supply risk, using the Kraljic matrix.
Strategic items have big spend and few good sources, like Bisi's school-colour check fabric. Build a close relationship, and approve a backup before a crisis.
Leverage items have big spend but many suppliers, like white shirting. Compare quotes and negotiate.
Bottleneck items are cheap but hard to get, like zips in the one colour the school demands. Running out stops delivery, so hold extra stock or find a second source.
Non-critical items, like thread, need as little thinking time as possible.
Specifications
Write a spec you can actually check
Approve a new supplier only after a small trial.
Name, type and grade
Appearance, smell and feel
Packaging and labelling
Keep a reference sample
Trial: measure the waste
Good shea butter means something different to every trader. A specification is a short written description of exactly what you accept.
For example, Funke writes: unrefined shea butter, for cosmetic use.
Ivory to pale yellow, smooth, no sand or water drops. Mild, nutty smell. Reject if sour or rancid.
Clean, sealed buckets with the packing date on the lid. And she keeps one 250 g jar from an approved delivery as the standard.
For a new supplier, she melts and strains 1 kg. The new butter left 100 g of grit, or 10% waste. Her approved supplier's was about 1%.
Use checks you can really do: look, smell, weigh, measure, or a small test batch.
Safety first
Safe buying rules
Chemicals: original sealed, labelled container
Ask for a safety data sheet where possible
Store chemicals away from food and children
New supplier: small trial order first
Pay only to an account matching the business
Keep every transfer receipt
If you buy chemicals such as caustic soda or acids, accept only the original sealed, labelled container, with a safety data sheet where possible.
Never accept a chemical in an unlabelled water bottle. Store chemicals away from food and out of children's reach.
Scammers pose as suppliers online. Start with a small trial, pay into an account whose name matches the business, and keep the receipt.
Key points
Remember
Your BOM shows where the money goes
Many shortages start at tier 2 or 3
One supplier means a single point of failure
Strategic items need a tested backup
A written spec makes quality checkable
To remember. Your bill of materials shows where your money goes. Many shortages start at tier 2 or 3. One supplier is a single point of failure.
Strategic items need a tested backup. And a written spec makes quality checkable.

Order on time, check every delivery, compare true cost
Order on time, check every delivery, and compare the true cost.
This is the video for module two of Supply Chain and Raw Materials Sourcing: planning, checking and costing your supply.
Why this matters
The working tools of a buyer
Most stockouts come from ordering too late
Problems found at the gate cost a phone call
Cheapest price is often not cheapest material
Price is only one thing to negotiate
Most stockouts are not caused by the supplier alone. They happen because the order was placed too late.
A problem found at the gate costs you a phone call. Found after production, it costs the whole batch.
And the cheapest price per kilogram is often not the cheapest material. You will learn to compare true cost, then negotiate.
Step by step
Find your reorder point
Your records set the lead time, not the supplier's promise.
Normal: 100 bottles x 5 days = 500
Worst case: 140 bottles x 8 days = 1,120
Safety stock: 1,120 minus 500 = 620
Reorder point: 500 + 620 = 1,120

The reorder point is the stock level that tells you: order now. You need three numbers. Usage per working day. Lead time, from placing the order to having checked, usable stock. And safety stock, the extra that covers bad weeks.
For example, Amaka fills an average of 100 bottles a day, and delivery takes 5 working days on average. So normal demand during lead time is 500 bottles.
On busy days she fills 140, and delivery took 8 days at worst. Worst case is 1,120 bottles.
Safety stock is the difference: 620 bottles. At about 60 naira each, that is 37,200 naira of cash tied up.
Her reorder point is 500 plus 620, which is 1,120. When her count falls to 1,120, she orders.
Use your last six to ten orders to find lead time. A supplier's promise of two days is not your lead time. Your records are.
At the gate
Doubtful stock goes to a HOLD area, never into production.
Match the paperwork with your order
Count cartons, weigh a few bags
Inspect seals and packaging
Check a spread-out sample against spec
Record date, supplier, batch, result
Compare the delivery note with your order. Then count and weigh on your own scale. A 25 kg bag that weighs 23.5 kg is short by 6%.
Check that seals are intact and labels readable. Open several containers from different parts of the load, not just the top one, and compare with your reference sample.
Then decide: accept, hold or reject, and write it down.
Put doubtful stock in a marked HOLD area. Photograph any problem before you move anything, and send the photos to the supplier the same day.
Safety first
Store materials safely
First in, first out; or first expired, first out
Off the floor, away from walls
Cool, dry and shaded
Chemicals and fuel well apart from food
Label material, supplier, date and batch
Store well. Put new stock behind old, and use materials with expiry dates in date order. Keep sacks on pallets or shelves, away from walls, to reduce damp and pests.
Heat and humidity spoil oils, sugar and flour. Keep chemicals, cleaning products and fuel well apart from food or cosmetic materials. And label every container.
Worked example
Total cost: two shea butter suppliers
For example, Funke compares two shea butter suppliers for an order of 25 kg.
A: 25 kg, free delivery
A: per usable kg (1% waste)
B: 25 kg plus transport
B: plus straining time
B: per usable kg (10% waste)
Prices are illustrative and approximate.
Total cost of ownership adds everything it costs to get a material into production: price, transport, waste, extra labour and late deliveries. Funke's prices are illustrative.
Supplier A charges 2,500 naira per kg with free delivery, so 62,500 naira. Only 1% is lost in straining, so each usable kilogram costs about 2,525 naira.
Supplier B charges 2,000 naira per kg, plus 7,500 transport, making 57,500. Extra straining time adds 2,000 naira, so 59,500.
But 10% is grit, so only 22.5 kg is usable. That is about 2,644 naira per usable kilogram.
The supplier that looked 20% cheaper is about 119 naira more expensive per usable kilogram, before counting late deliveries.
Negotiating
Price is only one lever
Price tiers at bigger volumes
Payment terms
Fixed delivery day
Replacement for failed material
Priority stock during shortages
Before you talk, know your best alternative, usually your approved backup supplier and their price. If you can buy at 2,550 naira elsewhere, you can calmly decline a rise to 2,700.
Ask about price tiers, payment terms and a fixed delivery day. Ask open questions, and let the supplier propose first.
Ask for replacement of material that fails your spec, and priority during shortages in return for regular orders.
If they move on price, trade something they value. Then confirm what was agreed in a WhatsApp message the same day.
Key points
Remember
Reorder point: normal demand plus safety stock
Check every delivery before production
Compare cost per usable unit, not sticker price
Your backup supplier is your strength
Pay only to the account name you confirmed
To remember. Order at your reorder point. Check every delivery before it touches production. Compare cost per usable unit, not sticker price. A tested backup gives you strength.
And if a supplier suddenly asks you to pay into a different account, call them on the number you already know before paying.

This is the video for module three of Supply Chain and Raw Materials Sourcing: growing a resilient supply chain.
Why this matters
Closer to the source, with less risk
Each layer adds a margin and a delay
Small producers can buy together
Delegate buying without losing control
Prepare for what could go wrong
Each layer between you and the source adds a margin and a delay. Buying closer can lower your price, but needs bigger orders, more cash earlier, and more risk on your side.
Buy direct only when your volume, cash and storage can carry it. If not, combine with other producers.
As you grow, you will also hand buying to someone else, and you will need a plan for when supply fails.
Worked example
Five cream makers buy together
For example, Funke and four other cream makers combine orders for 250 kg of shea butter.
Goods: 250 kg at 2,150
Transport for the whole load
Landed cost per kg
Funke pays, 80 kg
Kemi pays, 20 kg
Figures are illustrative and approximate.
Funke and four others each pay 2,500 naira per kg for 25 kg. A processor offers 2,150 naira per kg for 250 kg. Figures are illustrative.
The goods cost 537,500 naira, and transport for the whole load is 30,000 naira.
They share transport by weight: 30,000 divided by 250 is 120 naira per kg. So everyone's landed cost is 2,270 naira per kg, a saving of 230 naira.
Funke orders 80 kg and pays 181,600 naira, saving 18,400. Kemi orders 20 kg and pays 45,400.
The 567,500 naira collected exactly covers goods and transport, and each member saves about 9%.
Money safety
Group buying rules
Written agreement: spec, quantities, costs
Collect all money first, into one account
Share receipts in the group
Weigh each share on delivery, on video
Agree what happens if it fails the spec
Group money needs clear rules. Write a short agreement with the spec, each member's quantity, how costs are shared, and who holds the money.
Collect all money into one account before paying, and share receipts in the group. Weigh each share in front of members or on video, and agree in advance what happens if the material fails the spec.
Importing basics
Three risks when you import
Agree the Incoterm and named place in writing. Under CIF, risk passes to you at loading.
A 10% weaker naira turned 3,000,000 naira of goods into 3,300,000 naira.
Check SON and NAFDAC rules, use a licensed customs agent, verify the supplier, start with a sample.

Some materials are only available abroad. International trade uses Incoterms to state who pays and when risk passes. Always agree the term and the named place in writing. Under CIF, the seller pays freight, but risk still passes to you at loading.
There is also exchange-rate risk. For illustration, goods costing 3,000,000 naira cost 3,300,000 if the naira weakens by 10% before you pay. Build a margin for this.
Some imports must meet SON or NAFDAC rules. Speak with a licensed customs agent first. Never pay a foreign supplier you have not verified, and start with a sample shipment.
Delegating
Bisi's buying rules for her assistant
No single person orders, receives and pays alone.
Up to 50,000 naira, approved supplier: order
50,001 to 300,000: wait for written approval
Above 300,000 or new supplier: Bisi decides
Another person counts every delivery
Pay by transfer only after signed receipt
For example, Bisi hires Tunde to buy for her workshop, and they both sign one page of rules. Up to 50,000 naira from an approved supplier at the agreed price, he orders without asking.
From 50,001 to 300,000, he sends the quote on WhatsApp and waits for her written approval.
Above 300,000, any new supplier or any higher price, Bisi decides after at least two quotes.
Her senior tailor checks every delivery, and payment goes from the business account only after the receiving record is signed.
This is separation of duties. And anyone who buys for you must declare any personal link to a supplier, and report or refuse gifts.
Risk register
Score each risk: likelihood x impact
Bottle distributor fails: 4 x 5 = 20
Hibiscus price spike: 3 x 4 = 12
Sugar price rise: 4 x 3 = 12
Printer loses design file: 2 x 3 = 6

Resilience means keeping production going when something goes wrong. Score each risk from 1 to 5 for likelihood and for impact, and multiply. 15 or more needs action now, 8 to 14 needs a plan, and below 8 you watch.
For Amaka, her only bottle distributor failing for two weeks scores 20. She qualifies a second source and holds 620 bottles of safety stock.
Hibiscus and sugar price rises each score 12, so she plans for them, for example buying hibiscus earlier when prices are lower.
The printer risk scores 6, and she fixes it today in five minutes by saving her own copy of the file.
90-day plan
Reduce one big risk in 90 days
Days 1 to 15: find three options
Days 61 to 80: split orders, build stock
Days 81 to 90: review and choose next risk
Work on your highest risk first. In the first 15 days, find at least three possible suppliers and send your spec. Up to day 30, test samples against your reference.
Up to day 60, place real orders and measure lead time. Then split regular orders, for example 70% main and 30% backup.
By day 90, rescore the risk and choose the next one.
Key points
Remember
Buy direct only if volume, cash and space allow
Share group transport by weight
Agree the Incoterm in writing
Separate ordering, receiving and paying
Act first on the highest risk score
To remember. Buy direct only when volume, cash and space allow. Share group transport by weight. Agree the Incoterm in writing.
Separate ordering, receiving and paying. And act first on your highest risk.
